title: Swings and pendulums: how a swing trades height for speed

summary.text: Hold a bag of coins on a thread at the height of your chin and let it go. It never swings back higher than where it started. Stop its thread with a pencil halfway, so the bag has to swing in a much tighter curve, and it still climbs to the same height. Your child tests this with a thread and a bag of coins, then finds out how much harder a bag hits a box when it falls from higher up. They learn that height and speed are two forms of one thing, called energy, that a swing keeps trading back and forth. They also find out why a swing slowly dies down, why a push at the right moment makes it grow, and how to time a swing so the stopwatch error almost disappears.
summary.art: A bag of coins on a thread swinging past a pencil peg stuck out from a wall, with a horizontal pencil line on the wall showing that the bag rises to the same height on both sides.

intro.hook: Hold a bag of coins on a thread at the height of your chin. Let go, without pushing. The bag swings down and across, and climbs up the other side. Does it come back as high as your chin, higher, or lower? Now put a pencil in the way of the thread, so the thread catches on it halfway down. Will the bag still climb as high?
intro.text: An earlier unit on pendulums showed that the length of the thread sets the beat. This unit asks a different question. Where does a swing get its speed, and where does that speed go? Guess now whether the bag will climb as high when a pencil catches its thread, and write your guess down. You will test it in the first experiment, the Peg Test.
intro.art: A child's hand letting go of a bag of coins on a thread beside a wall with a pencil line marked at the starting height.

outcomes: I can explain that a swinging bob trades height for speed on the way down, and speed for height on the way up.
I can use the words height energy and movement energy, and say where each one is biggest in a swing.
I can predict that a bob climbs back to about the height it started from, even when a peg shortens the thread, and test it.
I can use the rule that a pendulum 1 metre long takes about 2 seconds for one full swing, and work out the time for other lengths.
I can explain why a swing slowly dies down but keeps the same beat, and why a clock needs a small push every swing.
I can explain how a person pumps a swing higher by moving their body at the right moment.
I can explain why timing many swings gives a better answer than timing one, and use a pendulum to find how strongly the Earth pulls.

terms.meaning: A weight hanging from a fixed point that swings freely back and forth.
terms.example: A playground swing, a hanging lamp and a bag of coins on a thread are all pendulums.
terms.art: A bag of coins on a thread hanging from a ruler, with a curved arrow showing the swing.

terms.meaning: The fixed point a pendulum hangs from and swings around.
terms.example: On a swing, the pivot is the hook at the top of the chains.
terms.art: The top bar of a swing with a circle around the hooks.

terms.meaning: The weight at the end of a pendulum.
terms.example: On a swing, the bob is the child on the seat.
terms.art: A small plastic bag twisted tight around five coins, tied to a thread.

terms.meaning: The time one full swing takes, there and back again.
terms.example: A pendulum 1 metre long has a period of about 2 seconds.
terms.art: A pendulum drawn at the left end, the right end and back at the left end, with a stopwatch.

terms.meaning: How far a pendulum swings from the middle to one end. A big amplitude is a wide swing.
terms.example: A gentle push gives a small amplitude. A big push gives a large one.
terms.art: A pendulum with a double-headed arrow from the middle to one end of the swing.

terms.meaning: How many full swings happen in one second. To find it, divide 1 by the period.
terms.example: A period of 2 seconds means a frequency of half a swing every second.
terms.art: A clock face with ticks and a count of swings in one second.

terms.meaning: What makes things move, heat up or change. Energy comes in different forms, and it can change from one form to another.
terms.example: A moving cricket ball has energy. So does a ball held high above the floor.
terms.art: A cricket ball in the air and another held high, each with a glowing outline.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is high above the ground and can fall. Scientists call it gravitational potential energy.
terms.example: A bag of coins held at chin height has more height energy than the same bag held at your waist.
terms.art: Two coin bags held at different heights, with the higher one glowing brighter.

terms.meaning: The energy a thing has because it is moving. Scientists call it kinetic energy. Faster things have more.
terms.example: A bag swinging fast at the bottom has more movement energy than a bag that has almost stopped.
terms.art: A coin bag with long speed lines at the bottom of its swing.

terms.meaning: The rule that energy is never made or destroyed. It only changes from one form to another.
terms.example: As a bob falls, height energy turns into movement energy, and the total stays the same.
terms.art: A bar split in two, with the height part shrinking and the movement part growing.

terms.meaning: The slow loss of a swing's energy to the air and the pivot, so each swing is a little smaller than the last.
terms.example: A swing in a park that nobody pushes swings lower and lower until it stops.
terms.art: A pendulum's path drawn as arcs that get smaller and smaller.

terms.meaning: When pushes come at a thing's own beat, each push adds to the last and the swing grows big.
terms.example: Pushing a friend on a swing each time they come back to you.
terms.art: A parent pushing a swing just as it reaches the top of its backward swing.

terms.meaning: The beat a pendulum keeps by itself when left alone. For a pendulum it is set by its length and the Earth's pull.
terms.example: A 25 centimetre pendulum has a natural beat of about one swing per second.
terms.art: A short pendulum and a long pendulum, each with its own beat marked as dots.

terms.meaning: The part of a clock that lets the wheels move on by one tooth with each swing, and gives the pendulum a tiny push each time.
terms.example: The anchor-shaped piece at the top of an old wall clock is an escapement.
terms.art: A toothed wheel with an anchor-shaped piece rocking above it.

terms.meaning: The point where all of a thing's weight seems to pull. It is the point where the whole thing balances.
terms.example: A ruler balanced on a pencil balances at its middle, its centre of mass.
terms.art: A ruler balanced on a pencil at its middle with a small dot at the balance point.

terms.meaning: The small mistake in a time that comes from pressing the stopwatch a little early or late.
terms.example: If you press late by a fifth of a second, a 1 second time looks 20 percent wrong, but a 30 second time looks less than 1 percent wrong.
terms.art: A finger above a phone stopwatch, with a small clock showing a time just past the real moment.

explanations.concept: Two forms of energy: height and movement
explanations.context: This card gives the two words you need to talk about a swing: height energy and movement energy.
explanations.definition: A thing high up has height energy, because it can fall. A moving thing has movement energy. A swing keeps swapping one for the other.
explanations.description: Hold a bag of coins high and let go. It falls, and the further it falls, the faster it goes. The height it had is turning into speed. Scientists call the energy of height gravitational potential energy, and the energy of movement kinetic energy. In this unit we say height energy and movement energy. Both are measured in joules. A thing held higher has more height energy. A thing moving faster has more movement energy. Mass matters too, because a heavy thing held at the same height has more of both. But for the swing, the bob's mass stays the same, so only height and speed change.
examples: A cricket ball held on the roof has height energy. After it falls, the same energy is in its movement.
A water tank on a roof has height energy. The water falls through the pipe and arrives at the tap with speed.
A child at the top of a slide has height energy. At the bottom the child has movement energy.
A swing at the end of its path has the most height energy. At the bottom it has the most movement energy.
explanations.art: A coin bag held high with a label height energy, and the same bag near the floor with long speed lines labelled movement energy.

explanations.concept: The swap: how a swing trades height for speed
explanations.context: This card explains where a swinging bob gets its speed and why it climbs again on the far side.
explanations.definition: On the way down, a bob loses height and gains speed. On the way up, it loses speed and gains height. The two add up to a total that stays almost the same.
explanations.description: Pull a bob to one side and you lift it, so it has height energy and no movement. Let go. Gravity pulls it down, height turns into speed, and at the very bottom the bob moves fastest. Then it rushes up the other side. Its speed turns back into height until it stops for a moment at the top. It stops at nearly the same height it started from, because the energy it had is still there. If it climbed higher, it would have made new energy from nothing. Nobody has ever seen this happen. The bob always comes back a tiny bit lower. A little energy leaks into the air as warmth.
examples: The chain swing in a park is fastest at the bottom, where you feel your tummy flip.
A bag of coins let go from chin height never touches your nose on its way back.
A marble rolled in a bowl climbs the far side to nearly the same height.
A skateboarder in a half-pipe rises to nearly the same height on both sides.
explanations.art: A pendulum drawn at five points of a swing, with a bar chart beside each showing height energy falling and movement energy rising, then the reverse.

explanations.concept: The peg: the path can change but the height stays
explanations.context: This card explains what you saw in the Peg Test, when a pencil caught the thread but the bob still climbed to the same height.
explanations.definition: A bob that falls from a certain height rises again to that same height, whatever path it takes on the way up, as long as nothing steals its energy.
explanations.description: Galileo showed this with a pendulum and a nail. He hung a ball on a thread and let it go from a certain height. The ball swung up the far side to the same height. Then he put a nail in the wall so the thread caught on it halfway down, and the ball had to swing in a smaller circle around the nail. It still rose to the same height as before. The path was different, the thread was shorter, and the swing was quicker. But the height did not change. What matters is how far the bob fell, not the path it took. This is why a roller coaster car can never climb a hill higher than the one it started from.
examples: A roller coaster car cannot climb a hill taller than the first hill, unless it gets another push.
A ball let go at the top of a curved slide rises to the same height up a steeper slide on the other side.
A bob on a thread with a peg swings faster around the short part but rises to the same height.
explanations.art: A pendulum released from the left with a peg halfway down the thread, and a dotted horizontal line showing the bob reaching the same height on the right.

explanations.concept: How long a swing takes: the rule for the period
explanations.context: This card gives a short rule for working out how long a pendulum of any length takes for one full swing.
explanations.definition: For a small swing, the period in seconds is about twice the square root of the length in metres. A pendulum 1 metre long takes about 2 seconds, and one 25 centimetres long takes about 1 second.
explanations.description: A square root is the number that, multiplied by itself, gives the number you started with. The square root of 4 is 2, because 2 times 2 is 4. The square root of a quarter is a half. A 25 centimetre pendulum is a quarter of a metre long. The square root of a quarter is a half, and twice a half is 1 second. For a 1 metre pendulum, the square root of 1 is 1, and twice that is 2 seconds. A 4 metre pendulum takes 4 seconds. To make a swing take twice as long, you need a thread 4 times as long. The full rule is that the period equals 2 times pi times the square root of the length divided by the strength of the Earth's pull. The weight of the bob does not appear in it at all.
examples: A pendulum of 25 centimetres takes about 1 second. One of 100 centimetres takes about 2 seconds.
A clock pendulum that ticks once a second each way is about 1 metre long.
A long swing on 4 metre chains takes about 4 seconds for a full swing.
explanations.art: A table showing lengths of 25 centimetres, 100 centimetres and 400 centimetres next to periods of 1, 2 and 4 seconds, with a pendulum drawn beside each.

explanations.concept: The Earth's pull sets the beat
explanations.context: This card explains why a pendulum swings more slowly on the Moon, and how a pendulum can measure the pull of the Earth.
explanations.definition: A pendulum's period depends on the length and on the strength of gravity. Where gravity is weaker, the same pendulum swings more slowly.
explanations.description: On the Moon, gravity is about one sixth as strong as on Earth. The same pendulum would take about two and a half times longer for each swing. So a pendulum can be used to measure gravity. Time a pendulum of known length, and the rule can be turned round to give the Earth's pull. In 1672, a French astronomer called Jean Richer took a clock with a pendulum to Cayenne, in South America, near the equator. He reported that it lost about two and a half minutes a day compared with Paris. The Earth pulls a little less near the equator, so the same pendulum swings a little more slowly. Today the strength of gravity near the Earth's surface is about 9.8 in units called metres per second per second.
examples: On the Moon a 1 metre pendulum would take about 5 seconds for a full swing, instead of 2.
A pendulum clock moved to a high mountain runs very slightly slow.
Geologists once used pendulums to look for rock structures hidden underground, because the pull differs by a tiny amount over them.
explanations.art: Two identical pendulums, one on Earth swinging in 2 seconds and one on the Moon swinging in 5 seconds, with the Moon one drawn with a lighter pull arrow.

explanations.concept: Why a swing dies down but keeps its beat
explanations.context: This card explains how a swing slowly loses its energy, and what a clock does to keep a pendulum going.
explanations.definition: A pendulum loses a little energy on every swing to the air and to the pivot. Each swing gets smaller, but the beat stays almost the same. A clock gives the pendulum a tiny push each swing to replace what it loses.
explanations.description: The air pushes back on the bob as it moves, and the pivot rubs a little. The energy these take turns into a tiny amount of warmth. So each swing is a little smaller, and after some minutes the pendulum stops. A small, heavy bob on a thin thread keeps going longest, because it pushes little air out of the way. The beat does not change as the swing shrinks, which is why clocks work. An old clock has an escapement, which lets a wheel move on by one tooth each swing and gives the pendulum a small push. The energy for these pushes comes from the weight or spring that powers the clock. In 1656 Christiaan Huygens built the first clock that used a pendulum this way, and it kept far better time than clocks before it.
examples: A coin bag in a quiet room swings for a long time. With a postcard taped to it, the bag stops much sooner.
An old wall clock needs winding every day or every week, depending on the clock, to keep its pendulum going.
A pendulum swung in water stops after a few swings, because water pushes back far harder than air.
explanations.art: A pendulum with smaller and smaller arcs drawn behind it, and an escapement above giving a small push at the bottom of each swing.

explanations.concept: Pumping a swing: adding energy with your body
explanations.context: This card explains how a person on a swing can go higher without anyone pushing.
explanations.definition: A person on a swing can add energy by standing up and crouching down at the right moments. This makes the swing act like a slightly shorter and then a slightly longer pendulum, in time with the swing.
explanations.description: A swing is a pendulum, and you are the bob. When you crouch at the highest point of each swing and stand up at the lowest point, you push your body up against the pull of gravity and of the swing. That push adds energy. The swing climbs higher with every pump. Sitting down and swinging your legs works in a similar way, because you move your centre of mass at the right moments. Moving your body at the wrong moments takes energy away. Scientists have worked out that the best timing is two pumps in each full swing: one at each end of the path. You can copy this with a coin pendulum and a straw. Pull the thread up through the straw when the bob passes the bottom, and let it out at the ends.
examples: A child on a park swing standing up at the bottom and crouching at the top.
A trapeze artist leaning at the right moments of each swing.
In the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Spain, a team of men pull the rope of a huge incense burner in time with its swing, to make it fly very high.
explanations.art: Three pictures of a child on a swing: crouching at the highest point, standing at the lowest point, and crouching again at the other end.

explanations.concept: Resonance in bigger things: pushes that add up
explanations.context: This card shows how small pushes at the right beat can build up in large things like bridges.
explanations.definition: A thing with a natural beat grows a big swing if it is pushed at that beat. This is called resonance. It can make a very big thing sway.
explanations.description: A swing has a natural beat. Small pushes at the same beat add up, and the swing grows. Bridges, buildings and even glasses have natural beats too. In June 2000, the Millennium Bridge across the river Thames in London opened to the public, and walkers made it sway from side to side. As it began to sway, the walkers started to step in time with the sway, which made it sway more. It was closed after two days and fixed with devices that damp the sway. Soldiers are told to break step on small bridges so their steps do not add up. The bridge was not weak. It simply had a natural sideways beat that crowds happened to match.
examples: Pushing a friend on a swing every time they come back to you.
Soldiers breaking step on a bridge.
A heavy pendulum near the top of a tall building, which swings against the sway of the building in an earthquake or high wind.
explanations.art: A footbridge with many people walking, swaying sideways in a curve, with a small arrow showing the sway growing.

explanations.concept: Stiff pendulums: when the whole thing swings
explanations.context: This card is about pendulums that are not a weight on a thread, such as your arm, a ruler or a leg.
explanations.definition: A stiff swinging thing such as a ruler is a pendulum too. Its weight is spread along its length, so it swings as if its length were shorter than it really is.
explanations.description: A ruler hung from one end swings like a pendulum, but the weight is spread out along it, not all at the bottom. The top half of the ruler is close to the pivot and wants to swing quickly. The bottom half is far from the pivot and wants to swing slowly. The ruler ends up swinging at a beat in between. A ruler hung from one end swings at about the same beat as a weight on a thread two thirds as long. A 30 centimetre ruler swings like a 20 centimetre pendulum. Your leg is a stiff pendulum too. This is why a person with long legs takes slower, longer steps. This is also why the centre of mass matters: it is the point where the weight of the whole thing seems to pull.
examples: A 30 centimetre ruler hung by its end swings like a 20 centimetre pendulum.
A gibbon hanging from a branch swings her whole body like a stiff pendulum.
Your arm swings freely when you walk, at about the same beat as your legs.
explanations.art: A ruler hung from a pencil by a hole at its end, next to a coin pendulum two thirds as long, both labelled with the same swing time.

explanations.concept: Timing many swings gives a better answer
explanations.context: This card explains why scientists time many swings, not one, and what that does to the mistake in a stopwatch time.
explanations.definition: Everyone presses a stopwatch a little early or late. That mistake is about the same size whether you time one swing or thirty, so it matters much less when the total time is long.
explanations.description: Say your reaction is a fifth of a second late each time you press the button. If you time a single swing of 1 second, your answer may be 20 percent wrong. If you time 30 swings that take 30 seconds, the same mistake is less than 1 percent of the total. Then you divide by 30 to get the time of one swing. This is why the tests in the earlier unit on pendulums timed 10 swings and not one. It is also why scientists repeat a test and use the mean, which is the total of the results divided by how many there are. An odd result that sits far from the others is worth checking again, and not just throwing away. Timing 100 swings would be even better, but a pendulum dies down, and your attention wanders. Choosing how many to time is a balance.
examples: A time of 1.3 seconds for one swing can be wrong by 0.3 seconds. A time of 30.4 seconds for 30 swings is only wrong by about 1 percent.
Divers, athletes and bakers repeat their timing for the same reason.
Scientists who keep the exact second today count the beats of atoms, billions of them, for the same reason: the more beats you count, the smaller the share of the mistake.
explanations.art: Two stopwatch faces, one showing a short time with a big red uncertainty bar and one showing a long time with a tiny red bar.

agreed.text: A thing high up has energy of height, and a moving thing has energy of movement. In a swing the two swap, and the total stays almost the same.
agreed.evidence: A bob let go from a height rises on the far side to almost the same height. This has been measured for centuries.

agreed.text: A bob rises to the same height it fell from, even if a peg changes its path.
agreed.evidence: Galileo described this test with a nail in his book of 1638. You can repeat it with a pencil and a bag of coins.

agreed.text: For small swings, a pendulum's period is about 2 times the square root of its length in metres.
agreed.evidence: Huygens worked out the rule in the 1600s. Anyone can check it with a stopwatch and a thread.

agreed.text: Gravity is weaker on the Moon, so the same pendulum swings more slowly there.
agreed.evidence: The period depends on the strength of gravity. Pendulum clocks also run very slightly slow on high mountains.

agreed.text: A pendulum slows because of the air and the rubbing at the pivot. A swing in a vacuum keeps going far longer.
agreed.evidence: Experiments with pendulums in a box with the air pumped out show that the swing dies down much more slowly.

agreed.text: A tiny push at the right beat makes a swing grow, and a push at the wrong time makes it shrink.
agreed.evidence: Anyone who has pushed a swing has felt it. It also explains the Millennium Bridge sway of 2000.

challenging.claim: A bob let go from a height can swing higher than the height it started from.
challenging.who: Many children, when they first see a pendulum swing fast
challenging.for: The bob is moving fast at the bottom, so it seems it should carry on higher.
challenging.against: The speed at the bottom came from the height the bob fell. On the way up that speed is used up again. In every test, the bob returns to a little below its start.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a swing can climb higher than its starting point without a push.

challenging.claim: Shortening the thread with a peg makes the bob rise higher on the far side.
challenging.who: Many people, when they first see the peg test
challenging.for: A shorter thread makes a tighter curve, so the bob seems to be thrown up higher.
challenging.against: The bob rises to the same height as before. The path is tighter and the swing is quicker, but the energy is the same.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that a shorter thread would throw the bob higher.

challenging.claim: A heavier bob keeps swinging much longer because it has more energy.
challenging.who: A common idea among children and some grown-ups
challenging.for: A heavier bob has more energy to lose, and heavy things feel harder to stop.
challenging.against: A heavier bob does last somewhat longer, but only when it is the same size as a lighter one. The air pushes on both with the same force, and the heavier bob has more energy to lose, so it takes the air longer to use it up. A big, light bob is stopped quickly, however much energy it starts with.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a heavy bob keeps swinging longer than a light bob.

challenging.claim: Time is something a pendulum makes.
challenging.who: Some people who see a clock tick
challenging.for: Clocks seem to produce time, tick by tick.
challenging.against: A pendulum only counts a steady beat that already exists because of its length and the Earth's pull. Clocks measure time. They do not make it.
challenging.context: This card is about whether a clock makes time or only measures it.

challenging.claim: Energy used by a swinging pendulum disappears.
challenging.who: A common idea about things that run down
challenging.for: The swing gets smaller and finally stops, so it looks as if the energy has gone.
challenging.against: The energy has not vanished. It has turned into a tiny amount of warmth in the air and in the pivot. Energy is never lost, only changed.
challenging.context: This card is about where the energy goes when a swing slows down and stops.

big_questions.q: A bob let go from chin height comes back to almost chin height, and never higher. Why can it not come back higher?
big_questions.hint: Think about where the speed at the bottom came from.

big_questions.q: With a peg, the bob swings a tighter path but reaches the same height. What does that tell you about what decides how high a bob climbs?
big_questions.hint: What stayed the same, and what changed?

big_questions.q: A pendulum four times longer takes only twice as long for each swing. Why does the time grow more slowly than the length?
big_questions.hint: A longer thread means a longer path, but also a gentler slope.

big_questions.q: Energy is never lost, only changed. When a swing stops, where did its energy go, and can it come back?
big_questions.hint: Think about the air the swing pushed through and the pivot it rubbed on.

big_questions.q: A child can pump a swing higher with no help from anyone. Where does the extra energy come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what the child's muscles did, and what gave them energy.

big_questions.q: Before pendulum clocks, how did people share one time between towns? What changed when clocks agreed?
big_questions.hint: Think about trains, markets and school bells.

big_questions.q: The Millennium Bridge was strong, yet a crowd made it sway. Can many small pushes, each harmless alone, add up to something big?
big_questions.hint: Think about the pushes at the right beat.

big_questions.q: A pendulum measures the pull of the Earth without touching the Earth. What else might we learn about a place by watching something small swing?
big_questions.hint: A clock moved to Cayenne lost time. What does that say about the ground under it?

story.title: Higher Than the Start
story.note: The story is made up. The science in it is real. A swing let go without a push never rises above its starting height. The best way to make it go higher is to move your body at the right moments, which is called pumping. Families in Karnataka and elsewhere hang swings from mango trees for festivals.
text: In the lane behind Anjali's house in Udupi, there was a mango tree with one thick branch that stuck out over the yard like an arm. Every summer holiday, her grandfather tied two ropes to that branch and fixed a plank between them. Anjali was nine, and this plank was the best thing in her whole year.
This summer, her cousin Vikram had come from Bengaluru. He was eleven, and he knew a great many things. He said so often.
"I can swing higher than this branch," he announced on the first morning, pushing the plank back with his hands. "Watch. One huge push, and I will go right over the top."
"You can't," said Anjali.
"Of course I can. I am much bigger than you."

Anjali thought about the school science lesson on pendulums. "Let's test it," she said. She fetched a piece of chalk from her school bag, and made a long mark on the wall beside the swing. It was exactly as high as the plank was when Vikram pulled it back and held it still. "This is where you start. Let go. Don't push. Then we look at where you stop on the other side."
"That's not fair. A swing needs a push!"
"If you push, it is your muscles that add energy. I want to see what the swing does by itself."

Vikram rolled his eyes, but he held the plank at the chalk line, and let go. He swooped down, fast, to the bottom, where his hair streamed back, and then up the other side. He slowed. He stopped, for a moment, and his face was pointing at the sky. Anjali was watching the chalk line. His feet had not reached it. He was just a finger-width below it.

"Again," said Vikram. He tried five times. Each time, the swing climbed up the far side to just below the chalk line, and never above it. Once, he leaned back, to make it go higher, and it did not help.
"It is as if the swing remembers how high it started," said Vikram, annoyed. "It never goes higher."

"It is only height turning into speed and back again," said Anjali. "When you fall, your height turns into speed. At the bottom you have all that speed. On the way up, the speed turns back into height. You can't get more height than you started with, unless somebody adds more energy."
"So I was right that I need a push."
"You were right that you need to add energy," said Anjali. "But I know a way to do it without anyone pushing."

Grandmother, who had been shelling peas on the verandah, put the bowl down and smiled. She did not say anything. She got up slowly, took hold of the ropes, and sat on the plank. Then, to Vikram's surprise, she began to swing. She did not kick her legs. She leaned back as the swing came up, and bent forward again as it fell. Her whole body moved in time with the plank. Each swing was wider than the one before. In five swings, her toes were higher than the lowest branches.
"Stand up at the bottom," Anjali called out, "and crouch at the top! That is how you add energy!"

Vikram watched. Then he took his turn. At first, he did it all wrong, and the swing jerked. Then he got it. When he reached the bottom, he stood up on the plank. When the swing reached the top, he crouched. The swing grew. It went up past the chalk line, which was above his head. His mouth fell open.
"It's higher than the line!" he shouted.
"Because you added energy," said Anjali. "With every crouch and stand, you put a bit of your own into the swing. The swing didn't make any itself."
That evening, Vikram lay in the hammock. "Anjali," he said slowly. "I was wrong about the swing. I thought being bigger would make it go higher."
"Being bigger helps your legs push harder," said Anjali. "But the swing only gives back what you put in."

The next morning Grandmother brought out a small brass bell on a string, and hung the bell from the tree, where a little breeze set the bell swinging. "This is the oldest clock in the house," she said. "It never stops, because the wind keeps pushing it at the right time." Anjali and Vikram sat beside it, and counted how often it swung in a minute.
story.epiphany: For the parent: a swing let go from a height cannot rise above that height on its own, because its speed at the bottom comes from the height it fell. A person can add energy by moving their body in time with the swing, which is called pumping. The energy comes from the person's own muscles.
ask: Why did the swing not reach the chalk line, even when Vikram leaned back?
What did Grandmother do that made the swing go higher without anyone pushing it?
Anjali said the swing only gives back what you put in. Is that always true, or can a swing lose some of it as well?
Where did the extra energy come from when Vikram pumped the swing?

games.title: Swap Shop: height energy or movement energy?
games.context: This is a card game about the energy swap in a swing. Each card shows a moment, and you decide which kind of energy is bigger at that moment.

setup.art: Twenty-four cards in a shuffled pile with two kinds of token in front of each player: Height and Movement.
setup.caption: 1. Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards into a pile.

setup.art: One child reading a card aloud while the others each put a token face down.
setup.caption: 2. The reader reads a card. Everyone else picks a token.

setup.art: The reader turning the card over to show the answer and the reason, with a point counter beside each player.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the tokens over together. Read the back. A right answer scores a point.

printables.title: 24 two-sided cards: a moment on the front, and the answer with the reason on the back

items.f: A bob is pulled aside and held still, ready to be let go.
items.b: Height energy. The bob is high and not moving at all, so all its energy is height energy.

items.f: A swing is at the very bottom of its path, moving fastest.
items.b: Movement energy. At the bottom the swing is lowest, so it has used up its height and has the most speed.

items.f: A swing reaches the end of its path and stops for a moment.
items.b: Height energy. At the top it has stopped moving, so all its energy is stored in its height.

items.f: A cricket ball is thrown straight up and is at the top, just before it falls.
items.b: Height energy. At the very top, the ball stops for a moment, so it has no movement energy.

items.f: The same cricket ball just before it hits the ground.
items.b: Movement energy. It has fallen all the way, so its height energy has turned into speed.

items.f: A child sits at the top of a slide and has not yet slid down.
items.b: Height energy. The child is high and still.

items.f: A child reaches the bottom of the slide at full speed.
items.b: Movement energy. The child is at the lowest point and moving fastest.

items.f: A water tank on a roof, full of water that is not moving.
items.b: Height energy. The water is high and still, and could fall.

items.f: Water rushing out of the bottom of a tall pipe.
items.b: Movement energy. The water has fallen down the pipe, and its height energy has turned into speed.

items.f: A roller coaster car is at the top of the first big hill, just starting to tip over.
items.b: Height energy. At the top of the hill the car is high and slow.

items.f: A roller coaster car is at the bottom of the first big hill.
items.b: Movement energy. The car is lowest and fastest.

items.f: A bag of coins hangs on a thread at rest, straight down.
items.b: Neither is changing. It is at its lowest point and still, so it has no extra height energy and no movement energy.

items.f: A pendulum bob passes through the bottom, then rises on the far side.
items.b: It swaps from movement energy to height energy. As it rises, its speed turns back into height.

items.f: A swing on its way down, halfway between the top and the bottom.
items.b: Both are present. Half of its height energy has already turned into movement energy.

items.f: A marble rolled up the side of a bowl and stopping at the highest point it reaches.
items.b: Height energy. At the very top the marble stops, so its speed has turned into height.

items.f: A child on a playground swing crouching at the top of the swing and standing at the bottom.
items.b: The child adds energy. Standing up at the bottom puts extra movement energy into the swing, so the swing climbs a little higher each time.

items.f: A pendulum bob in a peg test, swinging in a tight curve around a peg.
items.b: The same height energy at the top. With a peg, the bob rises to the same height as before, though its path is tighter.

items.f: A swing is let go from a height. The air slows it a little as it swings across and back.
items.b: The swing returns a bit lower. A little of its energy has become warmth in the air and the pivot.

items.f: A ball rolls down a ramp from a stack of 3 books, then rolls up a ramp on the other side.
items.b: It rises to nearly the same height. Its height energy turns to movement at the bottom, then back to height.

items.f: A skateboarder at the lip of a half-pipe, just before dropping in.
items.b: Height energy. The skateboarder is high up and still.

items.f: A skateboarder at the bottom of a half-pipe, moving fast.
items.b: Movement energy. The skateboarder is lowest and fastest.

items.f: A heavy ball and a light ball are let go together from the same height. Which is faster at the bottom?
items.b: Both have the same speed. Gravity pulls a heavier ball harder, but a heavier ball is also harder to speed up, so they arrive together.

items.f: A bag of coins is lifted to chin height, then to waist height. Which has more height energy?
items.b: Chin height. The higher the bag is held, the more height energy it has.

items.f: A gibbon swinging below a branch at the lowest point of her swing.
items.b: Movement energy. She is lowest and fastest, which is when she lets go to reach the next branch.

printables.title: 8 tokens: four that say Height and four that say Movement

rules: One player is the reader. The reader takes the top card and reads the front aloud. The reader does not show the back.
Every other player puts one token face down. Pick Height if you think the height energy is bigger. Pick Movement if you think the movement energy is bigger.
Everyone turns their token over together. Then the reader reads the back.
A player with the right token scores 1 point. A player who also says the reason before the back is read scores 2 points.
Some cards have no right token because the answer is that neither is changing, or that both are present. For these, say what you think. A good reason scores 1 point.
Pass the reader's job to the next player after four cards. The game ends when the pile is finished. The player with the most points wins.
To play alone, read a card, pick a token and say your reason out loud before you check the back. Score 1 point for each right answer. Try to beat 16 out of 24.

flow.do: Cut out the 24 cards and the 8 tokens. Shuffle the cards and put them in a pile. Give each player one token of each kind.
flow.say: These cards show moments in a swing or a fall. Each player gets two tokens, Height and Movement.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards and tokens. Shuffle the cards. Take two tokens.
flow.context: This is the first step of Swap Shop. You set up the cards and the tokens.
flow.parent: The cards are cut out with scissors, so a grown-up should help younger children. You can also fold the sheet and tear along the folds. Any two kinds of tokens work, for example two coins where heads is Height and tails is Movement. The game works for 1 to 4 players.

flow.do: Play one practice card together. Use the card about a swing at the very bottom of its path. Show how to turn the tokens over together.
flow.say: A swing is at the very bottom, moving fastest. Which kind of energy is bigger there? Choose a token and say why.
flow.kid: A swing is at the bottom. Which energy is bigger? Pick a token.

check.q: A swing is at the very bottom of its path, moving at its fastest. Which kind of energy is bigger?
check.why: At the bottom the swing is lowest, so it has the least height energy. It is moving fastest, so it has the most movement energy. If you picked height, think about where the speed came from: it came from the height the swing fell.

flow.context: In this step, you play one practice card to learn how the tokens work.

flow.do: Play the next twelve cards. For each card, ask each player for a reason first. Then read the back aloud.
flow.say: Pick your token and tell me why. Then we check the back. Who got a point? Who gave a good reason?
flow.kid: Pick a token. Say why. Then check the back.

ask.q: What do the cards with height energy have in common?
good: The thing is high up and not moving.
It is at the top and has stopped for a moment.

flow.parent: Listen for reasons that use both kinds of energy. A child who says 'it is fast, so movement' is right. A child who says 'it is high, so height' is right. Then ask what the other kind of energy is doing at that moment.
flow.context: In this step, you play the middle part of the game and give a reason for each guess.

flow.do: Play the last eleven cards. Look out for the cards where the answer is neither kind of energy, or both. Talk about why those cards are different.
flow.say: Some cards have no single answer. For these, say what is happening to the energy. Is it swapping, adding, or being lost?
flow.kid: Some cards have no single token. Say what is happening to the energy.

ask.q: What happens to energy when a swing slows down and stops?
good: It turns into warmth in the air and the pivot.
It is not lost. It changes into heat.

flow.context: In this step, you play the last cards, where the energy is swapping, being added or being lost.

flow.do: Add up the points. Then choose the card that surprised everyone most, and talk about why.
flow.say: Which card surprised you most? What did you think before, and what do you think now?
flow.kid: Which card surprised you most? Why?

ask.q: Which card changed your mind, and why?
good: The heavy and light ball, because they land together.
The peg card, because the height stays the same.

flow.context: This is the last step of Swap Shop. You count the points and talk about what surprised you.

experiments.title: The Peg Test: does a bob rise to the same height?
experiments.context: In this experiment you let a bag of coins swing, mark how high it starts, and see whether it climbs back to that height. Then you catch the thread on a pencil peg and see whether the height changes.
experiments.question: When a pencil catches the thread halfway and makes the bob swing a shorter, tighter path, does the bob still rise to the height it started from?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. With the peg, will the bag rise to the height it started from, higher, or lower? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bag of coins, the same thread and the same starting height every time. Only the length of the thread below the peg changes. Mark the starting height on the paper and compare where the bag stops on the other side.
results_table: Length of thread below the peg (cm)
Our guess for how high it rises
Highest point it reached on the far side (cm above rest)
Same, higher or lower than the start?

materials.item: strong sewing thread or thin string, about 70 centimetres
a 30 centimetre ruler, wooden or plastic
3 heavy books to hold the ruler down on the edge of a table
a small plastic bag with 5 coins of one kind in it, twisted tight and tied to the thread
a plain wall, door or cupboard side right behind the swing, with a sheet of paper taped on it to mark on (a cereal box is too short to reach the peg)
a smooth, round pencil or pen to use as the peg, and sticky or masking tape that peels off clean
a second ruler or a measuring tape
a pencil and the results table on paper
a phone propped on a book to film the swing from the side (optional, but it makes the height easy to read)

experiments.safety: Keep your face and feet away from the swing path. Let go gently without pushing. The peg must not stick out far enough to catch anyone's arm. Tape the pencil on with the blunt end sticking out and the sharp tip flat against the wall, never pointing at a face. Ask a grown-up before taping to a painted wall.

schedule.what: Build the pendulum. Test it with no peg, with a peg 25 centimetres above the bag and with a peg 12 centimetres above the bag. Look for the height the bag reaches each time.

experiments.record: For each test, write the highest point the bag reached on the far side. Draw the swing and the peg for the last test. Then circle whether the height was the same, higher or lower than the start.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the table with 10 centimetres over the edge and the books on top. 2. Tie the thread to the tip of the ruler. 3. Make the thread 50 centimetres long, measured from the ruler to the middle of the bag. 4. Push the table towards a plain wall or cupboard side. The ruler should point at it. Stop when the thread hangs about 3 centimetres from the wall. The bag will swing sideways, along the wall. Tape a sheet of paper on the wall behind the bag. 5. With the bag hanging still, hold a pencil level with the middle of the bag and mark the paper. 6. Mark a second line 6 centimetres above that.
flow.say: The ruler's tip is the pivot. The bag of coins is the bob. The first line on the paper is where the bag rests. The second line is where we will let go.
flow.kid: Hang the bag from the ruler. Put paper on the wall behind it. Mark two lines.
flow.parent: Use a wall or cupboard that is flat and does not move. A cereal box is too short to use: the peg has to sit 25 centimetres below the pivot, which is higher than a box standing on the floor. Keep the thread about 3 centimetres from the wall so the swing does not touch it, and tape the knot on the ruler so it cannot slide. Measure the lines from the middle of the bag. With 2 to 4 children: one lets go, one looks across at the paper, level with the line, and one writes. Swap after each test. With one child: the child lets go and you look across at the paper.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Peg Test. You build a pendulum with a height scale behind it.

flow.do: Ask your child for a guess and a reason for each of the three tests. Write the guesses in the table.
flow.say: We will let the bag go from the top line three times. First with no peg. Then with a peg that catches the thread halfway. Then with a peg lower down. How high will it rise each time? Why?
flow.kid: Guess first. Will the bag rise as high with a peg? Higher? Lower? Why?

ask.q: What do you think will happen with the peg? Why?
good: It will go higher, because the thread is shorter and it gets flung.
It will go lower, because the thread is shorter.
It will be the same, because it started at the same height.

flow.parent: Do not say which is right. Write down the reason as well as the guess. Many children guess higher, because a tighter curve feels like a flick.
flow.context: In this step, you guess what the bag will do before you test it.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bag at the top line. 2. Let go without pushing. 3. Watch where the bag stops on the far side. 4. Ask someone to look across at the paper, level with the line, and say which line the bag reached. 5. Do it three times. Write the highest point each time.
flow.say: Test one has no peg. Let go gently and do not push. Where does the bag stop on the far side? Is it at the top line, above it or below it?
flow.kid: Let the bag go without a push. Watch where it stops on the far side.
flow.parent: The bag should stop a finger-width or less below the top line. If it stops much lower, check that the thread is not rubbing and that the wall is not touching the bag. Looking from the side, level with the line, is the easiest way to see. To see it more clearly, film the swing from the side with a phone propped level with the line and pause the video at the top.
flow.context: In this step, you test the pendulum with no peg, to see how high it climbs on its own.

flow.do: 1. Tape the pencil to the wall so it sticks out 8 centimetres. Keep the blunt end out and the sharp tip flat on the wall. 2. Put it right under the pivot, 25 centimetres above the middle of the resting bag, so the hanging thread just touches it. 3. Hold the bag at the top line on the other side and let go. 4. The thread should catch on the pencil as the bag passes the bottom. 5. Mark where the bag stops. 6. Do it three times.
flow.say: Test two has a peg. The thread will catch on the pencil, and the bag will have to swing in a tighter curve. Where will it stop?
flow.kid: Tape on the pencil peg. Let go. Where does the bag stop?
flow.parent: The thread catches the pencil as the bag passes the bottom. The bag should rise to nearly the same top line, even though the swing is quicker. If the thread wraps round the pencil, the starting height is too high for the short part of the thread. Use a lower line. The thread rubs the pencil a little, so with a peg the bag may come back slightly lower than without one. That is friction taking a little energy, not a failed test. A smooth, round peg takes the least energy.
flow.context: In this step, you add a peg and test whether the bag still climbs to the same height.

flow.do: 1. Move the pencil lower, so the part of the thread below it is only 12 centimetres. 2. Let go from the top line, which is 6 centimetres up. 3. Mark where the bag stops. 4. Do it three times.
flow.say: Test three has the peg much lower. The curve is even tighter. Will the bag still reach the same height?
flow.kid: Move the peg lower. Try again. Does the bag still reach the line?
flow.parent: With 12 centimetres of thread below the peg, the bag swings on a small circle. It should still reach about 5 to 6 centimetres above the line where it rests. If it does not, check that the thread is not slack.

check.q: With the peg, the bag swung a tighter path. Where did it stop on the far side?
options: At nearly the same height as the start
check.why: The bag rose to nearly the same height, whether or not there was a peg. The path changed, but the energy did not. If you picked higher, you may have been watching how fast the bag moved, not where it stopped.

flow.context: In this step, you move the peg lower and test again. You write down what the bag does.

flow.do: Look at the table together. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: What did the peg change, and what did it not change? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: What did the peg change? What stayed the same? Say why.

good: What I think: the bag always climbs back to where it started. What I saw: with the peg, it still reached the line. Why: its height turned into speed and back again.

flow.context: In this step, you look at all your results and explain what they show.

experiments.title: Height and Hit: how far does a box slide?
experiments.context: In this experiment you let a bag of coins swing down and hit a small box. You find out how the height it falls from changes how far the box slides.
experiments.question: If you let the bag fall from a higher starting height, how much further does it push a box across the floor?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. If you double the height you let go from, will the box slide the same distance, twice as far, or four times as far? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same bag, the same thread, the same box and the same smooth floor every time. Only the height you let go from changes. Let go gently, without pushing, from heights of 5, 10 and 20 centimetres above the rest position.
results_table: Height we let go from (cm above rest)

materials.item: strong thread, about 90 centimetres, and a 30 centimetre ruler held down on a table edge by 3 heavy books
a small plastic bag with 5 coins of one kind in it, twisted tight
a small light box with a flat bottom, such as an empty matchbox or tea sachet box
a smooth floor, such as tiles, that the box slides on easily
a second ruler to measure heights, and a measuring tape for the slide
sticky tape and a marker to mark the starting spot
a pencil and the results table on paper
a calculator or paper to work out the mean

experiments.safety: Keep feet and faces out of the bob's path. Let go gently and catch the bag after it hits the box. A table edge can be sharp, so keep the ruler end away from your child's face.

schedule.what: Hang the bag so it just clears the floor. Let go from 5, 10 and 20 centimetres three times each, and measure how far the box slides.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. Work out the mean of the three slides for each height. Draw a bar chart of the means with one bar for each starting height.

flow.do: 1. Tie the thread to the ruler tip and make it long enough that the bag hangs 2 centimetres above the floor. 2. Put a spot of tape on the floor under the bag. 3. Lay the box on its side on the tape, with its end touching the hanging bag. 4. Put a second strip of tape on the floor in a line away from the box. 5. Stand the second ruler upright beside the bag. Mark the rest height of the bag's middle on it. Then stick tape flags 5, 10 and 20 centimetres above that mark.
flow.say: The bag is our swinging hammer. The box is what it hits. We measure how far the box slides along the floor.
flow.kid: Hang the bag so it just clears the floor. Put the box where it will hit.
flow.parent: The thread length depends on your table. Most tables are 70 to 75 centimetres high, so a thread of 65 to 70 centimetres works. The bag should hit the middle of the box's end. If the box tumbles, use a flatter box.
flow.context: This is the first step of Height and Hit. You hang the bag so it just clears the floor and hits a small box.

flow.do: Ask your child for a guess and a reason. Write the guess in the table.
flow.say: We will let go from three heights, 5, 10 and 20 centimetres. If we double the height, how far will the box slide? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. If you let go from twice as high, how far will the box slide?

ask.q: How far do you think the box will slide if the bag falls from twice as high? Why?
good: Twice as far, because it hits twice as hard.
Four times as far, because it speeds up more and more.
Just a little further, because the speed does not change much.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. The answer may surprise your child.
flow.context: In this step, you guess what the height will do to the slide, before you test it.

flow.do: 1. Hold the bag at 5 centimetres above rest. 2. Let go gently, without pushing. 3. Catch the bag after it hits the box. 4. Measure how far the box slid. 5. Reset the box and do it two more times.
flow.say: Let go gently, and catch the bag after the hit. Measure how far the box slid. Do it three times for each height.
flow.kid: Let go from 5 centimetres. Catch the bag. Measure the slide.
flow.parent: The first height may only push the box a few centimetres. That is fine. Measure from the tape to the front of the box. If the box and bag stick together, tape a small piece of card to the box end. With 2 to 4 children: one holds and lets go, one catches the bag, one measures the slide, one writes. Swap jobs when you change the height. If the box does not move at all at 5 centimetres, use a lighter box or a smoother floor.
flow.context: In this step, you test the lowest starting height and measure how far the box slides.

flow.do: 1. Now let go from 10 centimetres above rest, three times. 2. Then let go from 20 centimetres, three times. 3. Measure each slide and write it in the table. 4. Work out the mean for each height.
flow.say: Now the same test from 10 centimetres, then from 20. Measure every slide. What do you notice?
flow.kid: Test 10 centimetres, then 20. Measure the slides. What changes?
flow.parent: The slide usually grows about as fast as the height does, so 10 centimetres slides roughly twice as far as 5, though the results are untidy. The example chart is made up: your numbers depend on your floor and your box, so look at the pattern, not the exact numbers. A bumpy floor, a tipping box or a bag that hits off-centre all make the results untidy. That is why we take the mean of three tries.

check.q: When the bag started from a greater height, what happened to the slide of the box?
options: The box slid about the same distance
check.why: A greater height gives the bag more height energy, which turns into more speed and more movement energy at the bottom. A bag with more movement energy pushes the box further. If your results looked mixed, work out the mean for each height.

flow.context: In this step, you test the two higher starting heights and find the mean slide for each.

flow.do: Look at your bar chart. Ask your child to say what they think, what they saw and why.
flow.say: What did the height change? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: What did the height change? Say what you think, what you saw and why.

good: What I think: a higher start means a bigger hit. What I saw: the box slid further each time I doubled the height. Why: more height energy turned into more movement energy.

flow.context: In this step, you look at your chart and explain what it shows.

experiments.title: How Many Swings Should You Time?
experiments.context: In this experiment you time a 25 centimetre pendulum by timing 1 swing, then 10, then 30. You find out which gives the steadiest answer for the time of one swing.
experiments.question: If you work out the time of one swing by timing 1 swing, 10 swings or 30 swings, which way gives answers that are closest to each other?
experiments.predict: Before you start, guess. Which way will give the answers that are closest together: timing 1 swing, 10 swings or 30 swings? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: Use the same 25 centimetre pendulum, and pull the bag the same small distance aside every time. Only the number of swings you time changes. Press the stopwatch the same way each time, and do the same number of tries for each count.
results_table: Time of one swing (s) from each try
Smallest and biggest time of one swing (s)

materials.item: strong sewing thread, about 40 centimetres
a 30 centimetre ruler held down on a table edge by 3 heavy books
a small plastic bag with 5 coins of one kind in it, twisted tight
a phone stopwatch or a clock with a seconds hand
a second ruler or measuring tape
a pencil and the results table on paper
a calculator or paper for dividing

schedule.what: Set the pendulum to 25 centimetres. Time 1 swing five times, 10 swings five times and 30 swings three times. Work out the time of one swing each time.

experiments.record: Fill in the table. For each try, divide the total time by the number of swings. Write the smallest and the biggest answer for each count. Circle the count where they are closest.

flow.do: 1. Set up the coin pendulum on the ruler. 2. Make the thread 25 centimetres to the middle of the bag. 3. Practise one swing: pull the bag a hand-width aside, let go and count one when it returns.
flow.say: A 25 centimetre pendulum should take about 1 second for a full swing. We will find out how well we can measure that.
flow.kid: Make the thread 25 centimetres. Practise one swing. Count one when it returns.
flow.parent: One swing is there and back. The bag should return to the hand that let it go in about 1 second. Two people work best: one lets go and counts, the other works the stopwatch. With 2 to 4 children, each child is the timer for one count (1, 10 or 30 swings) and the others count and let go. Then compare whose answers are closest together.
flow.context: This is the first step of How Many Swings Should You Time? You build a short pendulum and practise counting a swing.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason. Write it down.
flow.say: We will time 1 swing, then 10, then 30. Which will give answers that are closest together? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. Which count gives the steadiest answer? Why?

ask.q: Which do you think will be steadiest, and why?
good: 30 swings, because a small mistake is a small part of a long time.
1 swing, because it is the simplest.
10 swings, because it is in the middle.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guess. Many children say 1 swing, because it feels the most careful.
flow.context: In this step, you guess which count will give the steadiest answer.

flow.do: 1. Time 1 swing, five times. 2. Start the watch as you let go. 3. Stop it when the bag returns. 4. Write each time in the table.
flow.say: Start the watch as you let go. Stop it when the bag comes back. This is the hardest one to time. Write down every time.
flow.kid: Time one swing. Do it five times. Write every time.
flow.parent: Typically you will see times between about 0.7 and 1.4 seconds. That wide spread is the point of the test. Do not throw away any time.
flow.context: In this step, you time a single swing five times and see how much the answers vary.

flow.do: 1. Time 10 swings, five times. 2. Count out loud. 3. Divide each time by 10. 4. Write the answer in the last column.
flow.say: Now time 10 swings. Count out loud. Then divide by ten to get the time of one swing.
flow.kid: Time ten swings. Do it five times. Divide each time by ten.
flow.parent: Expect each try to be about 10 seconds, within a few tenths. After dividing by 10, the answers typically fall between about 0.95 and 1.05 seconds.
flow.context: In this step, you time 10 swings, five times, and work out the time of one swing.

flow.do: 1. Time 30 swings, three times. 2. Count out loud and tick every five swings on paper. 3. Divide each time by 30.
flow.say: Now 30 swings. Tick every five on paper so you do not lose count. Then divide by thirty.
flow.kid: Time thirty swings. Do it three times. Divide each by thirty.
flow.parent: The swing may get smaller as it goes. That is fine, because the beat stays the same. If you lose count, start that try again.

check.q: Which count of swings gave answers for the time of one swing that were closest to each other?
check.why: A press of the button that is a fifth of a second early or late spoils a 1 second time a lot, but spoils a 30 second time very little. If your results look different, check your counting, because a lost count spoils a long time.

flow.context: In this step, you time 30 swings, three times, and compare all three counts.

flow.do: Look at the smallest and biggest time of one swing for each count. Ask your child to say what they found.
flow.say: Which count gave the smallest gap between the smallest and the biggest answer? Tell me what you think, what you saw and why.
flow.kid: Which count gave the smallest gap? Say why.

good: What I think: timing more swings is better. What I saw: the 30 swing times were closest together. Why: the stopwatch mistake is the same size, but a small share of a long time.

flow.context: In this step, you look at your results and explain why timing many swings works better.

activities.title: Marble in a Bowl: how high does it climb?
activities.context: This is a quick activity for noticing. You let a marble roll down one side of a bowl and watch how high it climbs on the other side. It gets you ready for the questions about pendulums.

materials.item: a large round steel bowl, a kadai or a deep plate
a marble (goli), a small steel ball or a heavy round bead
a ruler
a small piece of tape or a sticky note
a pencil and paper to write the heights

schedule.what: Roll the marble from three heights up the side of a bowl, measure how high it climbs on the other side, and notice what it does.

activities.record: Draw the bowl and the marble. Write the start height and the stop height for each of your three tries. Write one thing you noticed and one thing you wonder.

flow.do: 1. Place the bowl on a table or the floor. 2. Hold the marble against the inside near the rim. 3. Let go. 4. Watch where it climbs to on the other side.
flow.say: Hold the marble near the top edge and let it go. Where does it climb to on the other side? Does it reach the rim?
flow.kid: Let the marble go from near the rim. Watch how high it climbs.

ask.q: What do you notice about how high the marble climbs?
good: It goes almost as high on the other side.
It is fastest at the bottom.
It goes a little lower each time.

flow.context: This is the first step of Marble in a Bowl. You let the marble go and watch where it climbs to.

flow.do: Stick a small piece of tape inside the bowl where you let go. Try again from there. Then stick a second piece of tape on the other side where the marble stops. Hold a ruler upright beside the bowl and read the height of each piece of tape. Do it for three starting points: low, middle and near the rim.
flow.say: The first tape marks where the marble starts. The second marks where it stops. How high is each? Is the stop higher, lower or the same as the start?
flow.kid: Mark the start with tape. Mark where the marble stops. Measure both with a ruler. Do it three times.
flow.parent: The marble should reach almost the height it started from each time, about a finger-width below. In a very small steel bowl the marble may fly out over the rim, so start it lower. With 2 to 4 children: one lets go, one marks the stop, one measures, one writes. Swap after each try. Read heights from the side, level with the tape.
flow.context: In this step, you mark the starting height and watch whether the marble reaches it on the other side.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about a pendulum, and write it down for later.
flow.say: A marble in a bowl is a bit like a bag of coins swinging on a thread. Do you think the bag will climb back to where it started? Why?
flow.kid: Will a swinging bag climb back to where it started? Why?

ask.q: What is your guess about a swinging bag? Why do you think so?
good: Any guess with a reason. Keep it for the Peg Test.

flow.parent: Do not give the answer. Your child will test it properly in the Peg Test.
flow.context: In this step, you make a guess about a swinging bag, to test later.

setup.caption: 1. Mark the start with tape and hold the marble there.

activities.title: Pump the Pendulum: add energy with the thread
activities.context: In this activity you copy how a child pumps a swing. You pull the thread through a straw at the bottom of each swing, and see if the swing grows.

materials.item: strong sewing thread, about 80 centimetres
a drinking straw or the empty barrel of a used-up ball pen (refill taken out)
a small plastic bag with 5 coins in it, twisted tight and tied to the thread
a ruler or paper with marks, to measure how wide the bag swings

schedule.what: Hold a thread through a straw, start a small swing and pump it by pulling the thread at the bottom and letting it out at the ends.

activities.record: Write how wide the swing was at the start, after five swings alone and after ten pumped swings. Draw the thread, the straw and the bag, and show with an arrow when you pulled and when you let go.

flow.do: 1. Pass the thread through the straw. 2. Tie the bag to the lower end, so it hangs 40 centimetres below the straw. 3. Hold the straw upright in your left hand. 4. Hold the top end of the thread in your right hand.
flow.say: The straw is the pivot. The thread goes up through it, and your right hand can pull it up or let it out.
flow.kid: Thread the straw. Tie the bag on. Hold the straw up. Hold the top of the thread.
flow.context: This is the first step of Pump the Pendulum. You build a pendulum whose length you can change with your hand.

flow.do: 1. Start a small swing of about 10 centimetres. 2. Watch it for five swings without touching the thread. 3. Write down how wide the swing is at the start and after five swings.
flow.say: First we watch what the swing does on its own. It should stay about the same size, or shrink a little.
flow.kid: Start a small swing. Watch it for five swings. Does it grow?
flow.parent: The swing may shrink a little. That is normal. It shows the swing is not growing by itself.
flow.context: In this step, you watch the swing without pumping, so you have something to compare with.

flow.do: 1. As the bag passes the bottom, pull the thread up through the straw by about 3 centimetres. 2. As the bag reaches the end, let the thread slide down again. 3. Do this for ten swings. 4. Measure how wide the swing is now and write it next to the earlier numbers.
flow.say: Pull the thread up when the bag is at the bottom. Let it out when the bag is at the ends. Does the swing grow?
flow.kid: Pull the thread at the bottom. Let it out at the ends. Does the swing grow?
flow.parent: This takes practice. If the swing does not grow, pull faster at the bottom and let the thread out more slowly. The thread should not rub hard in the straw. Also try pulling the thread only on every other pass. Even if the swing grows only a little, the bag moves faster when you pull the thread in. This activity is fussy. It may take several tries, and it may not work every time. With 2 to 4 children, take turns pumping while one child measures, and see who makes the swing widest in ten swings. If the swing will not grow, go to a real playground swing and pump it by standing up at the bottom and crouching at the ends. It is the same trick.

check.q: When you pull the thread up at the bottom of the swing, where does the extra energy come from?
options: From your hand and arm, which pull on the thread
From the Earth's pull getting stronger
check.why: Your hand pulls the thread up against the bag's weight and the pull of its swing. That pull adds energy to the swing. If you picked the bag, remember that the bag cannot make new energy on its own.

flow.context: In this step, you pump the pendulum and see whether it grows.

setup.caption: 2. Pull the thread when the bag passes the bottom.

activities.title: The Ruler Pendulum: a stiff swinger
activities.context: In this activity you hang a ruler by its end and let it swing. You find the length of thread on a coin pendulum that swings in step with it. It shows what happens when the weight is spread along the whole pendulum.

materials.item: a 30 centimetre ruler (plastic or wooden) with a loop of thread or tape through the hole near one end, to be the swinger
a pencil
3 heavy books to hold the pencil down on the table with its end sticking out 5 centimetres over the edge
the coin pendulum on a thread, hung from a second ruler held down by 3 more heavy books on the table edge
a phone stopwatch
sticky tape (a lump on the pencil tip stops the loop sliding off)

schedule.what: Hang a ruler from a pencil and time 10 swings. Then find a thread length for the coin pendulum that takes the same time.

activities.record: Write the time for 10 swings of the ruler. Write the thread length that gave the same time. Draw both pendulums side by side.

flow.do: 1. Lay the pencil on the table with 5 centimetres over the edge. Press it down with the books. 2. Slip the thread loop on the ruler over the pencil end. Put a lump of tape on the tip of the pencil so the loop cannot slide off. 3. Pull the lower end of the ruler aside by one hand-width and let go. 4. Watch it swing.
flow.say: The pencil is the pivot. The ruler is the bob and the thread together. Will it swing faster or slower than a coin on a 30 centimetre thread?
flow.kid: Hang the ruler on a pencil. Let it swing. Is it quick or slow?

ask.q: Will the ruler swing faster or slower than a coin bag on a 30 centimetre thread? Why?
good: Faster, because the top half is close to the pivot.
Slower, because it is heavier.
The same, because it is the same length.

flow.parent: If your ruler has no hole, tape a loop of thread to one end. The loop must be loose so the ruler swings freely and does not rub the table. The ruler swings side to side along the table edge. With 2 to 4 children: one lets go and counts, one runs the stopwatch, one writes.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Ruler Pendulum. You hang a ruler by its end and guess how fast it will swing.

flow.do: 1. Time 10 swings of the ruler. 2. Do it twice. 3. Write both times in your record.
flow.say: Time 10 swings, twice. How long does the ruler take?
flow.kid: Time ten swings of the ruler. Do it twice.
flow.parent: A 30 centimetre ruler takes about 9 seconds for 10 swings. If it takes much longer, the ruler may be rubbing on the pencil.
flow.context: In this step, you time the swinging ruler.

flow.do: 1. Hang the coin bag from the second ruler on the table. 2. Try thread lengths of 30, 25 and 20 centimetres. 3. Time 10 swings each time. 4. Find the length that gives the same time as the ruler.
flow.say: Which thread length gives the same time as the ruler? Try 30, then 25, then 20. Which is closest?
flow.kid: Try three thread lengths. Which matches the ruler?

check.q: A 30 centimetre ruler hung by its end swings at the same beat as a thread about how long?
check.why: The ruler's weight is spread along it. The top part swings quickly and the lower part slowly, so it swings like a pendulum about two thirds as long. For 30 centimetres, two thirds is 20. If you chose 30, you treated the ruler's weight as if it were all at the bottom.

flow.context: In this step, you find the thread length that matches the ruler.
flow.parent: Typically 30 centimetres takes about 11 seconds for 10 swings, 25 about 10 and 20 about 9. Your times will differ by a few tenths. If two lengths look close, try 22 as well.

setup.caption: 1. Hang the ruler on a pencil. Let it swing.

setup.art: A coin pendulum on a 20 centimetre thread beside the swinging ruler, both with the same time on a stopwatch.
setup.caption: 2. Find the thread length that swings in step with the ruler.

activities.title: Swing in Water: a pendulum with much more drag
activities.context: In this activity you swing your bag of coins through water instead of air. You find out how much more the water slows it down.

materials.item: a bucket or deep tub, about 30 centimetres deep
water to fill it to about 5 centimetres from the top
a ruler on a table edge, held down by 3 books
strong thread long enough that the bag hangs in the middle of the water
a small plastic bag with 10 coins in it, air squeezed out and twisted tight so it sinks and the thread stays tight
an old towel for spills

activities.safety: Wipe up spills at once, because a wet floor is slippery. A grown-up should set up the bucket where nobody will trip on it. Never leave a young child alone with the bucket of water, and empty it when you have finished.

schedule.what: Swing the bag through the air and count how many swings it makes. Then swing it through water and count again.

activities.record: Write how many swings the bag made in air and in water before the swing was half as wide. Say how many times more swings there were in air. Draw the two paths.

flow.do: 1. Put the bucket on the floor under the table edge, with a towel under it. 2. Hang the bag so it dips into the bucket's middle when the bucket is full. 3. First, swing the bag with the bucket empty: pull it 10 centimetres aside and let go. 4. Count the swings until the swing is only half as wide, about 5 centimetres.
flow.say: First we swing the bag through air only. Count how many swings it makes before the swing is half as wide as when you started.
flow.kid: Swing the bag with the bucket empty. Count the swings.
flow.parent: In air the bag swings for a long time. If your child gets tired of counting, stop at 30 swings and write 30 or more. The thread is long, so the pivot should be above the bucket's middle. If your table is much shorter, the bag must still hang in the bucket's middle, with room under it.
flow.context: This is the first step of Swing in Water. You swing the bag through air and count the swings.

flow.do: Ask for a guess about the water swing. Write it down.
flow.say: Now we fill the bucket and swing through water. How many swings do you think it will make? Why?
flow.kid: Guess how many swings in water. Why?

ask.q: How many swings do you expect in water? Why?
good: Fewer, because water is thicker than air.
None, because the water would stop it.
The same number, because the bag has not changed.

flow.context: In this step, you guess what the water will do to the swing.

flow.do: 1. Fill the bucket with water so the bag is under the surface. 2. Pull the bag 10 centimetres aside. 3. Let go gently. 4. Count the swings until the swing is half as wide. Write 0 if it does not even swing back.
flow.say: Pull the bag aside and let go. Count how many swings it makes. What happens?
flow.kid: Pull the bag aside in the water. Let go. Count the swings.
flow.parent: In water the bag usually makes only one or two slow swings, or just creeps back to the middle. Water is much thicker than air, so it takes energy from the swing very quickly. If the bag floats up and the thread goes slack, squeeze out more air or add more coins. With 2 to 4 children: one pulls and lets go, one counts, one writes. Then work out how many times more swings the bag made in air than in water.

check.q: Why does a pendulum stop so much sooner in water than in air?
options: Water pushes back much harder than air
check.why: Water is about 800 times denser than air, so it pushes back much harder on a moving bag, and takes its energy away quickly. If you chose the bag getting heavier, remember that the weight of a bob changes the beat of a swing very little.

flow.context: In this step, you swing the bag through water and count.
