setup.caption: 1. Hang the bag so it dips into the bucket.

setup.art: The bag pulled aside in the water, with small curls of water behind it.
setup.caption: 2. Pull the bag aside, let go and count the swings.

projects.title: Weigh the Pull of the Earth: find gravity with a pendulum
projects.context: In this 2-day project you build a pendulum exactly 1 metre long and time 30 swings. Then you work out how strongly the Earth pulls, using the rule for the period.

materials.item: strong thread, about 1.5 metres
a small plastic bag with 5 coins in it, twisted tight
a metre ruler or a measuring tape
sticky tape
a door frame, a high shelf edge or a clothes-stand arm to hang the pendulum from
a phone stopwatch
a calculator and paper

projects.safety: A grown-up should hang the thread from the door frame or shelf, and no child should climb on a chair to do it. Keep faces and feet out of the swing path. Tie the door open and ask the family to use another route while the thread hangs, so nobody walks into it.

schedule.what: Hang a pendulum exactly 1 metre long from the pivot to the middle of the bag. Check that 10 swings take about 20 seconds.
Time 30 swings three times, find the mean, work out the time for one swing and then use the rule for the period to find how strongly the Earth pulls.

projects.record: Write the length of the pendulum, the three times for 30 swings and the mean. Show each step of your sum. Compare your answer with 9.8.

flow.do: 1. Tape the end of the thread to the top of a door frame or a high shelf edge. 2. Tie the bag to the other end. 3. Measure from the tape to the middle of the bag. 4. Move the knot until it is exactly 100 centimetres. 5. Tape the thread at the top so that it cannot slip.
flow.say: The pendulum must be exactly one metre from the pivot to the middle of the bag. Measure twice. Is it still 100 centimetres after taping?
flow.kid: Hang the thread from the top. Make it exactly 100 centimetres.
flow.parent: Choose a spot out of draughts, away from a fan or a window. The bag must swing freely in front of the door or shelf, not touch it. A swing of 10 centimetres either side is enough.
flow.context: This is the first day of the project. You build a pendulum exactly one metre long.

flow.do: Time 10 swings. It should take about 20 seconds. If it is quite different, check the length again.
flow.say: A one metre pendulum takes about two seconds for each swing. Ten swings should take about twenty seconds. Is yours near that?
flow.kid: Time ten swings. It should be about twenty seconds.

ask.q: Is your time close to 20 seconds? If not, what might be wrong?
good: The length may be wrong.
I may have counted a half swing as a whole swing.

flow.context: In this step, you check that your pendulum is close to a two second swing.

flow.do: 1. Time 30 swings and count out loud. 2. Do it three times. 3. Write all three times.
flow.say: Today we time 30 swings, three times. Tick every five swings on paper so that you do not lose count.
flow.kid: Time thirty swings, three times. Tick every five swings.
flow.parent: Each time should be close to 60 seconds. If one is far from the others, do it again. Do not guess a time you did not measure. With 2 to 4 children: one lets go and counts out loud, one runs the stopwatch, one ticks every five swings; swap for each of the three tries.
flow.context: This is the second day of the project. You time 30 swings, three times.

flow.do: 1. Add the three times and divide by 3 to get the mean. 2. Divide the mean by 30 to get the time of one swing. 3. Multiply that time by itself. 4. Divide 39.5 by that answer.
flow.say: Add the three times and divide by three. Then divide by thirty. Multiply the answer by itself. Then divide 39.5 by the result. That is the pull of the Earth.
flow.kid: Find the mean. Divide by 30. Multiply by itself. Divide 39.5 by that.
flow.parent: Worked example: 60.2 seconds for 30 swings gives 2.007 seconds for one swing. Multiplied by itself that is 4.03. Then 39.5 divided by 4.03 is 9.8. A calculator helps. Your answer will typically be within about 5 percent of 9.8, so anywhere from about 9.3 to 10.3 is a good result. The number 39.5 is 4 times pi times pi.

check.q: On another planet, a pendulum 1 metre long takes 2.1 seconds for one swing. Is the pull there stronger or weaker than the Earth's?
options: Stronger, because the swing is slower
Weaker, because the swing is slower
The same, because the length is the same
check.why: On Earth the swing takes about 2.0 seconds. A slower swing means the pull is weaker. If you chose stronger, remember that on the Moon, where the pull is weaker, the same pendulum swings more slowly.

flow.context: In this step, you use your times to work out how strongly the Earth pulls.

flow.do: Compare your answer with 9.8. Ask your child why it might be a little different, and what to change next time.
flow.say: Is your answer close to 9.8? If not, what might have made it a bit bigger or smaller? What could we do better?
flow.kid: Is your answer near 9.8? Why might it be a little off?

ask.q: Why might your answer differ from 9.8?
good: The length was not exactly 100 centimetres.
I lost count of the swings.
The swing was wide and took a little longer.

flow.context: In this last step, you compare your answer with the known value and think about why it might differ.

challenges.title: Three-Quarter Pendulum: where must the peg go?
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. You use a peg to make a pendulum that swings in exactly three quarters of the time it takes without the peg.
challenges.problem: A pendulum 36 centimetres long takes about 12 seconds for 10 swings. Place a peg so that 10 swings take about 9 seconds, which is three quarters of the time.
constraints: Keep the thread 36 centimetres long, from the pivot to the middle of the bag.
Use only a pencil as the peg, fixed to the wall or cupboard behind the swing.
Let go from only 2 centimetres above the rest position.
The bag must swing a little way each side of the peg, and not wrap round it.
materials: the coin pendulum on a ruler
a wall or cupboard side behind the swing, with paper taped on it
general: Fix the peg 27 centimetres below the pivot, so only 9 centimetres of thread is below it. The short side swings in half the time of the long side.
Time 10 swings with no peg first. This is the plain time. Then add the peg and time again.
Check that 10 swings take about three quarters of the plain time.
creative: Try a peg at other heights, and find the heights that make 10 swings take two thirds, or four fifths, of the plain time.
Use two pegs, so the thread wraps round one and then the other, and see how the time changes.
Make a table of peg height against 10-swing time, and draw a line graph.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own peg pendulum. Choose a time you want, build it, test it and write what you found. Does the rule for the period help you guess where to put the peg?

flow.do: Read the problem together. Time 10 swings of the 36 centimetre pendulum with no peg. This is the plain time.
flow.say: How long do 10 swings take without a peg? Now guess where the peg should go to make it three quarters of that time.
flow.kid: Time ten plain swings. Guess where the peg should go.

ask.q: Where do you think the peg should go? Why?
good: Lower down, because that makes the thread shorter.
Halfway, because three quarters is near half.

flow.context: This is the first step of the Three-Quarter Pendulum challenge. You time the plain pendulum and guess.
flow.parent: Set the pendulum up as in the Peg Test, hanging in front of a wall. With 2 to 4 children, each writes a guess for the peg height, then you test every guess and see whose is closest. Roles: one lets go, one times, one moves the peg.

flow.do: Fix the peg in your chosen place. Let go from 2 centimetres up. Time 10 swings twice. Move the peg and test again until you get close to 9 seconds.
flow.say: Place the peg and time 10 swings. Too slow? Put the peg lower. Too quick? Put it higher.
flow.kid: Place the peg. Time ten swings. Move the peg. Try again.
flow.parent: A lower peg leaves a shorter thread below it, so that side of the swing is quicker and the total time is shorter. The plain time is about 12 seconds. The target is about 9. Allow half a second either way. Your times will differ by a few tenths with the stopwatch, so any result between about 8.5 and 9.5 seconds is a success. Use a smooth peg so the thread slides.
flow.context: In this step, you move the peg until the time is close to three quarters of the plain time.

flow.do: Ask your child to explain why the answer works. Draw the pendulum with its peg.
flow.say: Half of each swing is on the long side, and half on the short. The short side takes half as long. Why does that give three quarters in all?
flow.kid: Why does the short side take half the time? Draw your design.

check.q: A peg is placed so that the short part of the thread is one quarter as long as the whole thread. How long does the swing on the short side take, compared with the swing on the long side?
check.why: A pendulum one quarter as long swings in half the time. The short side takes half as long as the long side. So one full swing takes one half plus one quarter, which is three quarters of the plain time. If you chose a quarter, you used the length ratio, not the square root rule.

flow.context: In this step, you explain the result and draw your design.

items.p: This picture shows a swing at its highest point on one side. Label where the height energy is biggest and where the movement energy is biggest in the whole swing.
a: height energy is biggest at the two ends
movement energy is biggest at the bottom
items.why: At the ends the bob is highest and stops for a moment, so it has the most height energy. At the bottom it is lowest and fastest, so it has the most movement energy.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These words come up all through the unit. A strong answer could give a swing example of each.
pairs: the time for one full swing, there and back
how far the bob swings from the middle to one end
the slow loss of a swing's energy to the air and the pivot
pushes at the swing's own beat adding up
the clock part that gives the pendulum a small push each swing

items.p: Sort these moments. Is the height energy or the movement energy the bigger one?
items.why: A thing that is high up and still has mostly height energy. A thing that is low and fast has mostly movement energy.
items: a swing stopped for a moment at the end of its path
a swing passing the bottom of its path
a stone at the top of its throw
a stone just before it lands
a child at the top of a slide, about to go
a child at the bottom of the slide

items.p: A swing that nobody pushes can rise higher than the place it was let go from.
items.why: False. The speed at the bottom came from the height it fell. It can climb back to nearly the same height, but never higher, unless somebody adds energy.

items.p: A heavy bob and a light bob on the same length of thread swing at about the same beat.
items.why: True. The weight of the bob does not change the time of a swing. Gravity pulls a heavy bob harder, but it also needs more force to get moving, so the two cancel.

items.p: A swing is moving fastest at the ______ of its path.
items.why: It has fallen as far as it can, so all its height energy has become movement energy there.

items.p: A swing slowly dies down because the air and the pivot take a little of its ______ every swing.
items.why: Each swing a little of the energy turns into warmth in the air and at the pivot. It is not lost, only changed.

items.p: Put these moments of one swing in order, starting with the bob held at the left end.
a: Held still at the left end
Slowing down as it climbs the right side
Stopped for a moment at the right end
items.why: Height energy turns into movement energy on the way down, and movement energy turns back into height energy on the way up.
items: Stopped for a moment at the right end
Held still at the left end
Slowing down as it climbs the right side

items.p: Draw a bob swinging past a peg. Draw a dotted line to show how high it starts and how high it reaches on the other side.
items.a: The dotted line is at the same height on both sides, even though the path on one side is tighter.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the bob reaching the same height with and without the peg.
items.art: A blank pivot with a hanging thread, a peg halfway down, and space on both sides for the bob's path.

items.p: Explain why a bag of coins let go from chin height does not come back higher than chin height.
items.a: The bag falls, and its height turns into speed. At the bottom it has all that speed. As it climbs, the speed turns back into height. It can only get back the height it gave up, so it stops near the start.
items.why: A strong answer says that the speed came from the height, so the bag can only rise as high as it fell.

items.p: A friend says that a swing that has stopped has lost its energy for good. Do you agree? Say what happened to the energy.
items.a: I disagree. The energy has turned into a tiny amount of warmth in the air and at the pivot. Energy is never lost, only changed.
items.why: A strong answer names warmth, and says that the energy was changed, not destroyed.

items.p: A 1 metre pendulum takes about 2 seconds for one swing. About how long does a 25 centimetre pendulum take?
items.why: 25 centimetres is a quarter of a metre, and the square root of a quarter is a half. Twice a half is 1 second. If you chose 0.5, you used a quarter of the time, not its square root.

items.p: In a pendulum, what do you change to make each swing take longer?
items.why: Only the length of the thread changes the time much. The bob's weight and a bigger start change it very little.

items.p: At the very top of a swing the bob stops for a moment. What kind of energy does it have then?
items.why: It is not moving at that moment, so it has no movement energy. It is at its highest, so all its energy is height energy.

items.p: Why does timing 30 swings give a better answer for the time of one swing than timing 1 swing?
opts: The pendulum swings faster when it is timed longer
The stopwatch mistake is the same size, but a small share of a long time
The pendulum is heavier after a long time
items.why: Everyone presses the button a little early or late. That mistake is about the same size each time, so it spoils a long time much less than a short one.

items.p: Two cousins, Dhruv and Farida, argue about a park swing. Dhruv pushes the swing once and lets it go.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Farida. The swing cannot rise above the place it was let go from without an extra push. It gives Dhruv his due: a bigger push does make the swing go higher.
items.why: This question checks that the child knows a swing gets its height from where it is let go, and that pushing adds energy.

views.says: If the swing is going fast at the bottom, it will go higher than where I let go.
It can only climb back to where it started. The speed at the bottom came from the height.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use what you saw in the Peg Test, where the bag of coins was let go without a push. Then say one thing the other cousin has right.

items.p: A bob is let go from 10 centimetres above rest. A peg shortens the thread. The bob rises to which height on the far side?
items.why: The path is tighter but the bob has the same energy. It rises to nearly the same height. A little energy is lost to the air.

items.p: A pendulum takes 4 seconds for a full swing. About how long is it?
items.why: A period of 4 seconds is twice the square root of the length. So the square root of the length is 2. The length is 2 times 2, which is 4 metres. If you chose 16, you squared 4.

items.p: On the Moon, gravity is about a sixth as strong as on Earth. What happens to a pendulum of the same length?
opts: It swings about two and a half times more slowly
It swings at the same beat
It does not swing at all
items.why: A weaker pull gives a slower swing. The period grows with the square root of 6, which is about 2.5.

items.p: In the Height and Hit test, the bag falls from twice the height. What is true about its speed and the slide?
opts: The bag reaches the bottom faster, and the box slides further
The bag reaches the bottom at the same speed
The box slides exactly the same
items.why: A bag let go from higher has more height energy to turn into movement energy. It hits harder and pushes the box further.

items.p: Which of these swings keeps going longest after one start?
opts: A big flat card on a thread
A small, heavy bob on a thin thread
items.why: A small heavy bob pushes little air out of the way compared with its weight. The others push a lot of air, and lose energy quickly.

items.p: A pendulum 25 centimetres long takes about ______ second for one full swing.
items.why: A quarter of a metre has a square root of a half. Twice that is 1 second.

items.p: To make a pendulum take twice as long for each swing, you make its thread ______ times as long.
items.why: The period grows with the square root of the length. Twice the time needs 4 times the length, because the square root of 4 is 2.

items.p: A push at the wrong moment on a swing can make it go lower.
items.why: True. If you push while the swing is moving towards you, you take energy from it. A push at the right moment adds energy.

items.p: A pendulum clock makes time.
items.why: False. The pendulum has its own steady beat set by its length and the pull of the Earth. A clock counts that beat and shows it on hands. It does not make time.

items.p: Describe what happens to the energy of a bob in one full swing, starting from the moment you let go.
items.a: It starts with all height energy. As it falls, the height turns into movement energy. At the bottom it has the most movement energy. As it climbs, the movement turns back into height. At the far end it is all height again. A tiny bit leaks into warmth each swing.
items.why: A strong answer names both kinds of energy, shows that they swap, and notes the small loss to warmth.

items.p: A child on a park swing stands up at the bottom of each swing and crouches at the top. Explain why the swing goes higher.
items.a: The child pushes up against the swing at the bottom, when it moves fastest. That push adds energy to the swing. The extra energy comes from the child's own muscles.
items.why: A strong answer says that the child adds energy with their own muscles, not that the swing makes it by itself.

items.p: Three friends, Latha, Imran and Pooja, talk about why a pendulum finally stops.
items.a: A strong answer agrees most with Pooja, because the air and the rubbing at the pivot take the swing's energy and turn it into warmth. It gives Latha her due: gravity keeps pulling, but it pulls the bob back to the middle and does not stop it. It gives Imran his due: the movement has indeed gone, but it was changed into warmth.
items.why: This question checks that the child can use the idea of energy changing form to judge three ideas fairly.

views.says: The movement just ran out and disappeared.
The air and the pivot took the energy and turned it into a tiny bit of warmth.

items.ask: Whose idea explains it best? Say what each of the others got partly right.

items.p: Three of these change the time of a swing very little. Which one changes it a lot?
items.why: The length of the thread sets the beat. The weight of the bob, the number of coins and a slightly wider start change it very little.
opts: Using a different kind of coin
Making the thread four times longer

items.p: Three of these show a thing trading height for speed. Which one is about something else?
items.why: A ball rolling down a slide, a roller coaster dropping and a marble rolling inside a bowl all trade height for speed. A kitchen scale weighs rice, and does not trade height for speed.
opts: A ball rolling down a slide
A roller coaster dropping from its first hill
A marble rolling inside a bowl

items.p: Draw a graph of the height energy and the movement energy of a bob during one swing from the left end to the right end. Use two lines.
items.a: The height energy line is high at the ends and low in the middle. The movement energy line is low at the ends and high in the middle. They mirror each other.
items.why: A strong drawing shows the two lines swapping, with the total staying the same.
items.art: A blank graph with a horizontal line for position along the swing, a vertical line for energy and no data.

items.p: Put these in order, from the shortest period to the longest period.
items.why: A longer pendulum has a longer period. The periods are 1, 2, 3 and 4 seconds.

items.p: The Moon's pull is about a sixth of the Earth's. A pendulum clock is moved from Earth to the Moon. What does it do?
items.why: A weaker pull means a slower swing. The clock counts the swings, so it counts fewer swings per hour and shows less time than has passed.

items.p: A pendulum 36 centimetres long takes 1.2 seconds for a full swing. How long does a full swing of a pendulum 9 centimetres long take?
items.why: A pendulum a quarter as long swings in half the time, and half of 1.2 seconds is 0.6 seconds. If you chose 0.3, you took a quarter of the time instead of using the square root.

items.p: A swing set has two swings, one with 2 metre chains and one with 1 metre chains. Both are pushed with the same size of push. Which takes longer for one full swing?
opts: It depends on the weight of the child
items.why: A longer pendulum has a longer period. The weight of the child changes it very little.

items.p: A tall building has a heavy pendulum near the top that swings against the sway of the building in strong wind. What does it do?
opts: It adds energy to the sway
It takes energy from the sway
It holds the building still by weight alone
items.why: When the building sways, the pendulum swings the other way, taking energy from the sway. This is damping.

items.p: A pendulum takes 60.6 seconds for 30 swings. What is the time of one swing?
items.why: 60.6 divided by 30 is 2.02, about 2 seconds. This pendulum is about 1 metre long.

items.p: The strength of the Earth's pull is about ______ metres per second per second.
items.why: Falling things speed up by about 9.8 metres per second every second near the Earth's surface.

items.p: A pendulum clock that runs slow can be put right by moving the bob ______.
items.why: A shorter pendulum swings quicker. Moving the bob up makes the pendulum shorter, so the clock runs faster.

items.p: In 1672 Jean Richer reported that a pendulum clock lost time in Cayenne, near the equator, compared with Paris.
items.why: True. The Earth pulls a little less near the equator, so the same pendulum swings a little more slowly and a clock loses time.

items.p: Your pendulum answer for the pull of the Earth is 9.4 instead of 9.8. Give two reasons why, and say which you think is more likely.
items.a: The length may have been a little off, or a swing may have been miscounted. The timing error is more likely if only a few swings were timed. A wide swing also takes slightly longer. I think a lost count is most likely.
items.why: A strong answer gives at least two sources of error and links them to how the measurement was made.

items.p: Why can a pendulum clock keep time in a train that is moving at a steady speed, but not in a train that is turning hard round a bend?
items.a: In a steady train the pendulum swings just as in a house. In a hard bend the sideways push changes how the bob is pulled, so the beat changes. A steady motion does not change the swing.
items.why: A strong answer says that steady movement is invisible to the swing, but extra pushes change it.

items.p: The Millennium Bridge in London swayed when many people walked across on its first days. Explain with the word resonance.
items.a: The bridge had a natural sideways beat. Walkers' steps began to match the sway, and each push added to the last. The sway grew until the bridge was closed and fixed.
items.why: A strong answer connects resonance to pushes at the natural beat adding up.

items.p: Two students, Meera and Karan, discuss whether the Peg Test proves that energy is never lost.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Meera that the test shows the bob returning to nearly the same height. It gives Karan his due: the bob came back slightly lower, so some energy did leave. A strong answer says that the energy turned into warmth, and the test alone cannot show that.
items.why: This question checks that the child can say what a test shows and what it does not show.

views.says: The bob always came back to nearly the same height, so energy is conserved.
It came back a little lower each time, so some energy was lost.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? What would you add to the test to find out where the missing energy went?

items.p: Three of these would make a pendulum clock run faster. Which one would make it run slower?
items.why: A shorter pendulum swings quicker. A longer pendulum swings slower, so the clock runs slow.
opts: Taking a little off the thread
Shortening the rod with the nut

items.p: Draw a pendulum, a peg and the two paths of the bob on either side of the peg. Label the long side and the short side, and write how their times compare.
items.a: The long side is drawn as a wide arc, the short side as a tighter arc. The short side is labelled as a quicker half-swing.
items.why: A strong drawing shows both paths reaching the same height and labels which half is quicker.
items.art: A blank pivot with a hanging thread and a peg at the three-quarter point, with space for two arcs.

items.p: A Foucault pendulum shows that the Earth turns.
items.why: True. A very long pendulum keeps swinging in the same direction while the Earth turns underneath it, so its path seems to turn slowly. Léon Foucault first showed this in Paris in 1851.

quiz.p: A bob is let go without a push from a certain height. What is the highest it can reach on the other side?
opts: About the height it started from
Half the height it started from
It depends on the weight of the bob
quiz.why: Its height turned into speed and then back into height. It can only get back about what it gave up, a little less because of the air.

quiz.p: Where does a swinging bob have the most movement energy?
opts: At the highest point on the left
At the highest point on the right
At the bottom of its path
Halfway between the bottom and the top
quiz.why: At the bottom it has fallen as far as it can, so it is moving fastest. All its height energy has become movement energy.

quiz.p: A thread catches on a peg and makes a bob swing a tighter path. How high does the bob rise on the far side?
opts: To the same height as it started
To the height of the peg
quiz.why: The path changes but the energy does not. The bob rises to nearly the same height it started from.

quiz.p: A pendulum 1 metre long takes about 2 seconds for a full swing. How long does a 4 metre pendulum take?
quiz.why: A pendulum 4 times as long takes twice as long, because of the square root. Twice 2 seconds is 4 seconds.

quiz.p: A swing in a park slowly gets lower and lower if nobody pushes. What happens to its energy?
opts: It turns into a tiny amount of warmth in the air and pivot
It goes back into the ground as height
quiz.why: The air pushes against the swing and the pivot rubs. The energy that these take turns into warmth. It is changed, not lost.

quiz.p: A child on a swing stands up at the bottom of each swing and crouches at the top. What happens to the swing?
opts: It goes higher, because the child adds energy
It goes higher because the Earth pulls harder
quiz.why: The child's muscles push against the swing at the right moments, and that adds energy. The swing climbs higher.

quiz.p: You time 30 swings of a pendulum and divide by 30. Why is this better than timing 1 swing?
opts: The stopwatch is more exact for long times
The stopwatch mistake is a much smaller share of a long time
quiz.why: The mistake from pressing the button is about the same size each time. It is a big share of 1 second and a small share of 30 seconds.

quiz.p: A bag of coins swings down and hits a box. Then the bag is let go from twice the height. What happens to how far the box slides?
opts: The box slides about the same
quiz.why: A higher start gives more height energy, which turns into more movement energy at the bottom. The bag hits harder.

quiz.p: The same pendulum is taken to the Moon. What happens to its beat?
opts: It swings more slowly, because the Moon's pull is weaker
It swings faster, because the Moon is smaller
It swings at the same beat
quiz.why: The Moon pulls about a sixth as strongly as the Earth. A weaker pull gives a slower swing.

quiz.p: A 30 centimetre ruler hung by its end swings like a pendulum of about which length?
quiz.why: The ruler's weight is spread along it, so it swings like a pendulum about two thirds as long as the ruler.

quiz.p: Why does a clock give its pendulum a small push every swing?
opts: To replace the energy the pendulum loses to the air and the pivot
To change the length of the pendulum
quiz.why: Without the push, damping would make the swing shrink and stop. The energy for the small pushes comes from the clock's spring or weight.

quiz.p: Soldiers break step when crossing a small bridge. What is the reason?
opts: Their steps might add up at the bridge's natural beat and make it sway a lot
They are told to be quiet
quiz.why: Steps at the bridge's own beat add up, as pushes do on a swing. This is resonance. Breaking step stops the pushes from adding up.

Tall buildings with a huge pendulum near the top that swings against the sway caused by the wind, to keep the building steady.
Searching for heavy rocks or oil underground by measuring tiny differences in the pull of the Earth.
Foucault pendulums in science museums, which show that the Earth turns.
Cranes and wrecking balls, where engineers must plan for the swing of a hanging load.
Newton's cradle toys, which pass energy along a row of swinging balls.
Walking robots that let their legs swing like pendulums to save energy.

open_questions.q: What is energy, really? Is it a thing, or only a number that stays the same?
open_questions.why_open: Physicists can calculate with energy very exactly. Some, such as Richard Feynman, said that nobody knows what energy is, beyond a number that stays the same.

open_questions.q: Why does the Earth's pull on a thing always match exactly how hard the thing is to get moving?
open_questions.why_open: That is why a heavy and a light bob swing at the same beat. Einstein's general relativity explains it, but physicists still test it to higher and higher accuracy, and look for tiny differences.

open_questions.q: Is the pull of gravity the same everywhere in the universe and at all times?
open_questions.why_open: The strength of gravity is one of the least precisely known numbers in physics. Different careful experiments give slightly different answers.

open_questions.q: Could a perfect clock exist that never loses a second?
open_questions.why_open: Atomic clocks lose less than a second in hundreds of millions of years, but nobody knows if there is a limit to how steady a clock can be.

open_questions.q: How much energy do animals save by letting their limbs swing like pendulums?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have studied gibbons and walking humans, but the exact saving and how animals tune it is still being researched.

open_questions.q: Why do many separate swinging things, such as metronomes on a moving board, slowly fall into step?
open_questions.why_open: The simple case can be explained, but how similar things fall into step in fireflies, heart cells and crowds is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the Height and Hit test, a box slid 14 centimetres, 16 centimetres and 15 centimetres from the same starting height. What was the mean slide?
maths.explain: Add the three slides: 14 plus 16 plus 15 is 45. Divide by 3. 45 divided by 3 is 15. The mean slide was 15 centimetres.
maths.context: In the Height and Hit test, you let a bag fall on a box three times from each height and measured how far the box slid.
maths.why_maths: A test never gives exactly the same number twice, so the mean of three tries gives a fairer answer than a single try.

maths.problem: A pendulum is 64 centimetres long, which is 0.64 of a metre. The square root of 0.64 is 0.8. Using the rule that the period is twice the square root of the length in metres, how long do 10 swings take?
maths.explain: Twice 0.8 is 1.6, so one swing takes 1.6 seconds. Ten swings take 10 times 1.6, which is 16 seconds.
maths.context: In this unit you met a rule for how long a pendulum takes to swing, using the square root of its length.
maths.why_maths: A rule lets you predict a time before you test, and then you can check the prediction against your stopwatch.

maths.problem: In the Height and Hit test, doubling the height the bag falls from makes the box slide about twice as far. In one example, the box slid 7 centimetres when the bag fell from 5 centimetres up, and 15 centimetres when it fell from 10 centimetres up. About how far would you expect the box to slide when the bag falls from 40 centimetres up?
maths.explain: From 10 to 20 centimetres the slide roughly doubled again, to about 30. From 20 to 40 centimetres it doubles once more, to about 60. Each time the height doubles, the slide about doubles.
maths.context: In the Height and Hit test, you let a bag fall from different heights and measured how far a box slid.
maths.why_maths: Spotting that doubling the height doubles the slide lets you predict a result you have not tested.

maths.problem: A stopwatch press is a fifth of a second late. What share of the time is that mistake if you time 1 swing that takes 1 second, and what share if you time 30 swings that take 30 seconds?
maths.answer: For 1 second, the mistake is 1 fifth of the time, which is 20 percent. For 30 seconds, it is a fifth of a second out of 30 seconds, which is less than 1 percent.
maths.explain: A fifth of a second out of 1 second is one fifth, or 20 percent. A fifth of a second out of 30 seconds is 0.2 divided by 30, which is about 0.007, less than 1 percent. The same mistake is 30 times smaller as a share.
maths.context: In the experiment How Many Swings Should You Time?, you timed 1, 10 and 30 swings of a short pendulum and compared the answers.
maths.why_maths: Working out the share of the time that a mistake takes up shows why timing many swings gives a steadier answer.

maths.problem: Your pendulum took 60 seconds for 30 swings. How long did one swing take?
maths.explain: One swing is one thirtieth of the total time. 60 divided by 30 is 2. One swing took 2 seconds.
maths.context: In the project on the pull of the Earth, you time 30 swings of a pendulum 1 metre long.
maths.why_maths: Dividing the time for many swings by the number of swings gives the time of one swing with a much smaller mistake.

maths.problem: A wall clock loses 2 minutes every day. After how many days is it 10 minutes behind? Why would a clockmaker move the bob up?
maths.answer: After 5 days. Moving the bob up makes the pendulum shorter, so the clock runs faster.
maths.explain: Every day it falls 2 minutes further behind. 10 divided by 2 is 5 days. A shorter pendulum swings quicker, so moving the bob up makes the clock catch up.
maths.context: A pendulum clock counts its swings. If each swing is a little too slow, the clock slowly falls behind.
maths.why_maths: Working out how a small daily error builds up shows why clock makers care so much about tiny changes in a pendulum's length.

maths.problem: A 1 metre pendulum takes about 2 seconds for each swing on Earth, and about 5 seconds on the Moon. How much longer do 10 swings take on the Moon than on Earth?
maths.explain: On Earth 10 swings take 10 times 2, which is 20 seconds. On the Moon they take 10 times 5, which is 50 seconds. 50 take away 20 is 30 seconds.
maths.context: The Moon pulls about a sixth as strongly as the Earth, so a pendulum swings more slowly there.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the times of 10 swings in two places shows how much a weaker pull slows a pendulum down.

maths.problem: You want a pendulum that takes 3 seconds for one full swing. Half of 3 is 1.5. Multiply 1.5 by itself. How long should the pendulum be?
maths.explain: The period is twice the square root of the length, so the square root is half the period, which is 1.5. The length is 1.5 times 1.5, which is 2.25 metres.
maths.context: In this unit you used a rule that links the length of a pendulum to its time for a full swing.
maths.why_maths: Turning the rule around lets you work out the length you need for a swing time you want.

roots.context: In this unit you followed energy through a swing and tested how high a bob climbs. This part asks what the swap between height and speed tells us about the world, and about ourselves.

deep_truth.truth: In the Peg Test, a pencil peg shortened the thread, yet the bag still climbed to the same height. How high a bob climbs depends on how far it fell, not on the path. Its height turned into speed on the way down, and the speed turned back into height on the way up. So the path can change a lot while the height stays the same.
deep_truth.habit: We think the path decides where something ends up, so a tighter, quicker curve should fling the bob higher. In a swing the path does not matter. Only the height it fell from sets the height it reaches.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Peg Test, the bag reached about the same height with no peg, with a peg 25 centimetres above it and with a peg 12 centimetres above it. If your results differ, write them down as they are and test again.

three.who_am_i: When you walk, each step lifts your body a little and lets it fall forward again, like an upside-down pendulum. Your body gets back much of the energy of each step.
three.what_is_life: A gibbon in the forests of Assam swings under a branch and lets her height turn into speed, then speed into height, to reach the next branch. Much of the energy she needs to get there comes back to her from the swing itself.
three.what_is_this_world: Water lifted by the Sun falls as rain, a river runs down and a swing rises again. Height and movement keep trading places, and the total energy stays the same.

roots.thread: A bob held at the end of its path has height and no speed. At the bottom it has speed and no extra height. At the other end it has height again. The energy is never gone. It only changes from height to speed and back. A swing, a river, a roller coaster and a falling leaf all make this same swap, so the same few rules govern very different things. We can follow the energy through each of them, and it always adds up.

teachings.teaching: That is whole, this is whole. From the whole the whole comes out. Take the whole from the whole, and the whole remains.
teachings.link: As the bob falls, height energy is taken away and turns into movement energy. The total that remains is the same.

teachings.teaching: The road up and the road down are one and the same.
teachings.link: The bob goes down and up along the same arc. Falling and rising are two halves of one swing.

teachings.teaching: The Way of heaven is like bending a bow. What is high is lowered, and what is low is raised.
teachings.link: A swing lowers its height to raise its speed, and then lowers its speed to raise its height again.

science.text: Energy is never made or destroyed, only changed from one form to another. In 1918 Emmy Noether showed why: it follows from the fact that the laws of nature are the same from one moment to the next.
Some physicists think the total energy of the whole universe may be exactly zero, with the energy of matter cancelled by the energy of gravity. Nobody knows for sure.

other_view.view: In his lectures, Feynman said that physics has no knowledge of what energy actually is. He compared it to counting a child's building blocks: you always get the same number, even when some blocks are hidden. Energy, he said, is a number we calculate that stays the same, not a thing we can point at.

practice.title: Watch the turning point
practice.say: Hang the bag of coins and start a small swing. Sit still and watch only the ends of the swing. At each end the bag pauses for a moment. Breathe in slowly as it rises. Breathe out slowly as it falls. Do this for ten swings. Notice the stillness at each end, and the speed in between.
practice.kid: Start a small swing. Watch only the ends. Breathe in as it rises. Breathe out as it falls. Do it ten times.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, challenge and project was walked through as if at home, with the materials listed. The pendulum hangs from a ruler held down by books on a table edge, so it works in a flat. The Peg Test uses a wall or cupboard behind the swing as a height scale (a cereal box is too short), and the bag should reach about a finger-width below the starting line each time. Height and Hit needs a smooth floor and a thread long enough for the bag to clear the floor, usually 65 to 70 centimetres on a normal table. Doubling the height should roughly double the slide, but results are untidy, so the steps say to take the mean of three. The timing test needs about 30 minutes and works best with two people. The pumping activity is fussy and is marked as a try. The 1 metre pendulum for the pull of the Earth should typically give a value within about 5 percent of 9.8. Facts to check before printing: the Richer clock loss in Cayenne, the opening dates of the Millennium Bridge and the 1851 Foucault demonstration. The spine fits about 95 minutes.

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out how much energy a moving thing has? This card tells how a Dutch scientist and a French scientist found out, using brass balls and clay.
how_we_found_out.story: About three hundred years ago, many scientists followed Descartes, who said that the force of a moving thing is its weight times its speed. By that rule, a ball falling at twice the speed would dig twice as deep. A Dutch scientist, Willem 's Gravesande, tested it. He dropped brass balls into soft clay from different heights. A ball that fell from four times the height reached twice the speed, and it dug four times as deep, not twice. The result was puzzling. A French scientist, Emilie du Chatelet, read about his tests and studied them closely. In her book of 1740 she argued that the measure of a moving thing's force grows with the square of its speed. Double the speed, and the force of the hit becomes four times as big. This idea became the movement energy we use today. It also explains why the box in the Height and Hit test slides so much further when the bag falls from higher.
how_we_found_out.who: Willem 's Gravesande, a Dutch scientist, and Emilie du Chatelet, a French scientist (1706 to 1749)
how_we_found_out.when: The clay tests were in the 1720s. Her book was published in 1740.
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Scientists following Descartes held that a moving thing's force grows in step with its speed. The clay tests showed that it grows with the square of the speed.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist in an 18th-century room dropping a brass ball from a height into a dish of soft clay while a woman scholar watches and takes notes.
